A morning cup of coffee, a slice of apple, a spoonful of chocolate spread: all of these depend on creatures that most of us hardly notice. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), three out of four crops grown for human food depend, at least in part, on pollinators such as bees, butterflies and bats. (12)______. Pollinators are nevertheless in trouble. Experts point to habitat destruction and the use of pesticides, and close to a third of invertebrate pollinators, particularly bees and butterflies, face extinction. (13)______. For smallholder farmers who grow crops such as cocoa or coffee, fewer pollinators could mean lower incomes and a greater risk of hunger. (14)______. FAO notes that, with better management, pollination can even raise crop yields and quality. (15)______. Planting flowers, using fewer pesticides and protecting natural habitats are simple steps that help. (16)______.
(Adapted from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and Our World in Data)

A decade ago, an electric car was a rare sight on most roads, and many drivers doubted that it would ever

the petrol engine. Today the picture looks very different. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global electric car sales rose by around 20 per cent in 2025 to exceed 20 million, roughly one in four of all new cars sold worldwide. Electric cars set new sales records in close to a hundred countries.

China leads the market by a wide margin: Chinese manufacturers were responsible for about 60 per cent of electric car sales in 2025. Europe recorded the strongest growth among the major markets, with sales rising by more than 30 per cent. Emerging economies are catching up too. In Southeast Asia, electric car sales grew by nearly 50 per cent in 2024, and the share of electric cars in new sales is notably higher in Thailand and Viet Nam than elsewhere in the region.
Several factors explain this rapid growth.
Batteries have become cheaper and better, and new cell designs now allow faster, higher-voltage charging.
Governments have supported buyers with subsidies, tax breaks and emission rules.
The number of public charging points has also increased quickly, rising by about 40 per cent in 2023 alone.

Challenges remain, however. In the United States, battery electric cars were still about 30 per cent more expensive than conventional models in 2024, which dampened sales growth. Higher tariffs could raise prices further, while lower oil prices would reduce the fuel savings that attract buyers. Such uncertainties are real, but
have not changed the overall direction: the IEA expects electric cars to exceed 40 per cent of global sales by 2030 under today's policy settings.
(Adapted from the International Energy Agency's Global EV Outlook reports)
Chinese carmakers accounted for most of the world's electric car sales in 2025

When people hear the word "heritage", they usually picture temples, citadels and ancient tombs. Yet UNESCO also protects a different kind of treasure that cannot be touched: songs, festivals, rituals and craft skills passed from one generation to the next. This intangible cultural heritage lives only as long as people continue to practise

Vietnam is rich in such traditions. Quan họ folk singing, inscribed by UNESCO in 2009, is performed as alternating verses between women from one village and men from another, who answer with the same melody but different lyrics. Ca trù, a form of sung poetry with fifty-six different melodies, was placed on the list of heritage in need of urgent safeguarding in the same year.
Being recognised, however, does not guarantee survival, because a tradition lives on only when young people are willing to learn it.

Safeguarding therefore means more than keeping records. Practitioners pass on their skills in clubs, festivals and family homes, and UNESCO encourages governments to work closely with the communities concerned rather than act alone. The plan to safeguard ca trù, for instance, was praised because it relies on the
knowledge that still exists among those who practise it.

Some scholars warn that the process has risks. If heritage is managed only from the top down, they argue, it may be frozen into a fixed version that serves national pride but leaves little room for artists to experiment. Their concern does not mean that efforts to
old art forms are mistaken; it means that communities, and not only officials, should have a say in how a tradition evolves.

describing how to visit famous monuments
complaining that UNESCO ignores ancient tombs
introducing a kind of heritage that people cannot touch
